result:
That's not quite right, actually — language models don't remember on their own. Each call to the model is stateless: it only knows what's sitting in the context window you send it that moment. Nothing carries over automatically.

Any "memory" you've seen in a chatbot is the app around the model doing extra work: it saves facts somewhere (a file, a database) and pastes them back into the prompt next time it talks to that model. The model itself has no idea a week passed — it's like a new instance waking up each time, handed a note of what it's allowed to know.

It's an easy mistake because the *experience* feels continuous — ChatGPT "remembers" your name, so it feels like the model is doing the remembering. But that's the product layer, not the model.

For your makerspace assistant: if you want it to recall that a student finished laser-cutter training last week, your team has to build that — store the student's training status (probably a simple database lookup keyed by student ID), and have the agent fetch it and drop it into context before answering. That's a tool call or a retrieval step you design, same as the booking-calendar check in your agent loop — it doesn't come free with the model.

Kind of a kitchen analogy, since you cook: the model's like a line cook with amnesia between shifts. If the restaurant wants the cook to know "table 4 is allergic to peanuts," someone has to write it on a ticket and hand it over each time — the cook isn't retaining it on their own.

Does that distinction — model stateless, app does the remembering — make sense? If so, what do you think your assistant should store about each student between visits, and where?
